title: Letter from AO Director Robert J. Conrad Jr. to Senate Judiciary Chairman Grassley on the federal Judiciary's use of AI (with the AI Task Force interim guidance summary)
pub: Administrative Office of the United States Courts
author: Robert J. Conrad Jr.

dom.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision

st.t: AI evidence: Reliability differs from deepfake authenticity
st.an: Conrad supports the cluster’s principal framing by treating deepfake authenticity and AI-generated opinion reliability as distinct evidentiary issues. He also confirms that Rule 707 was only proposed for consultation, while broader procedural reform remains conditional on demonstrated gaps in existing rules and courts retain existing misconduct powers.
qs: challenges: (1) whether changes to the authenticity rules are necessary to deal with “deepfakes”; and (2) whether a change is needed to give courts authority to regulate opinion evidence that is the product of machine learning when no expert witness is proffered to testify.

In addition, although there are no pending proposals to address AI concerns before the Advisory Committees on Civil Rules, Criminal Rules, Appellate Rules, and Bankruptcy Rules, this is an issue that may receive attention in the future if a determination is made by the appropriate Committees that existing procedural rules do not adequately address concerns raised by the use of AI in court proceedings.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The federal Judiciary guidance directly supports the cluster’s assistive, human-accountable model: it cautions against delegating core judicial functions, requires independent human verification, and retains accountability for AI-assisted work. Its contextual approach to disclosure and locally approved tasks also aligns with the cluster’s account of jurisdiction-specific governance.
qs: The interim guidance cautions against delegating core judicial functions to AI,

It recommends that users review and independently verify all AI-generated content or output, and it reminds judges and Judiciary users and those who approve the use of AI that they are accountable for all work performed with the assistance of AI.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source directly supports institution-wide lifecycle supervision: it preserves core judicial functions for humans, requires independent verification and accountability, and embeds oversight, confidentiality, security and education in Judiciary-wide guidance. Its context-sensitive approach to disclosure and temporary policy development is consistent with the cluster’s qualified governance framework.
qs: It recommends that users review and independently verify all AI-generated content or output, and it reminds judges and Judiciary users and those who approve the use of AI that they are accountable for all work performed with the assistance of AI.
The guidance includes recommendations around oversight of and accountability for AI use, confidentiality and security of Judiciary data, and AI education, among other areas.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The letter supports the cluster’s core position by emphasizing that judges already possess disciplinary, contempt and procedural powers to address attorney misconduct, while treating additional AI-specific rules as conditional on demonstrated inadequacies in existing rules. Its proposed evidence rule also reflects targeted, task-specific governance rather than blanket AI restrictions.
qs: In addition to the ability to refer concerns to state disciplinary authorities, judges have authority through their contempt power and the rules of procedure to address attorney misconduct.

In addition, although there are no pending proposals to address AI concerns before the Advisory Committees on Civil Rules, Criminal Rules, Appellate Rules, and Bankruptcy Rules, this is an issue that may receive attention in the future if a determination is made by the appropriate Committees that existing procedural rules do not adequately address concerns raised by the use of AI in court proceedings.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: Conrad directly supports the cluster’s proposition that legal AI use should proceed through controlled institutional governance rather than blanket trust or prohibition. The federal Judiciary’s interim approach permits experimentation while preserving judicial independence, requires independent verification and human accountability, and treats disclosure as context-dependent. The letter documents guidance and ongoing policy development, not demonstrated effectiveness.
qs: The guidance aims to allow for the use of and experimentation with AI tools while preserving the integrity and independence of the federal courts and the judicial process.

It recommends that users review and independently verify all AI-generated content or output, and it reminds judges and Judiciary users and those who approve the use of AI that they are accountable for all work performed with the assistance of AI.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Conrad’s account supports the cluster’s core supervised-AI proposition: users should independently verify AI output, remain accountable for AI-assisted work, exercise heightened caution in adjudication and novel legal questions, and define permitted uses by task. It also aligns with context-dependent disclosure and reliance on existing ethical and procedural safeguards. The source does not assess whether verification costs consume efficiency gains.
qs: It recommends that users review and independently verify all AI-generated content or output, and it reminds judges and Judiciary users and those who approve the use of AI that they are accountable for all work performed with the assistance of AI.
More broadly, the guidance encourages courts to consider defining the tasks for which locally approved AI tools may be used.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The guidance directly supports selective, use-context-specific deployment: courts should define permitted AI tasks, exercise heightened caution in adjudicative and novel legal uses, and require independent human verification and accountability. It provides an institutional application of the cluster’s core proposition without materially extending or challenging it.

kp.k: Judiciary responds to growing AI use with advisory governance
kp.d: Conrad reports that standalone platforms and AI integration into legal research tools are making AI more common in legal work. He identifies potential judicial benefits alongside ethical, opinion-integrity, sensitive-data and IT-security risks. He established an advisory AI Task Force earlier in 2025, comprising judges, court unit executives, IT personnel and chambers staff across court types, to identify issues and recommend policies; the letter does not quantify adoption or benefits.
qs: With the increasing use of AI platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and integration of AI functions in legal research tools, AI use has become more common in the legal landscape.

AI presents a host of opportunities and potential benefits for the judicial branch, as well as concerns around maintaining high ethical standards, preserving the integrity of judicial opinions, safeguarding sensitive Judiciary data, and ensuring the security of the Judiciary’s IT systems.
The Task Force has been charged with identifying the issues that AI presents for the judicial branch and recommending new or updated policies accordingly.

kp.k: Interim guidance permits experimentation while permanent policies develop
kp.d: The Task Force’s interim guidance was broadcast Judiciary-wide on July 31, 2025, for federal judges, chambers staff and other Judiciary personnel. Conrad describes non-technical recommendations on AI use, procurement, security, oversight, accountability, confidentiality and education. These are temporary, non-exhaustive guideposts intended to support experimentation while protecting judicial integrity and independence, rather than a completed permanent policy framework.
qs: The Task Force developed interim guidance on the use of AI, which were broadcasted Judiciary-wide on July 31, 2025.
The guidance, which is intended for all federal judges, chambers staff, and other Judiciary personnel, contains general, non-technical suggestions on the use, procurement, and security of AI tools.
The guidance aims to allow for the use of and experimentation with AI tools while preserving the integrity and independence of the federal courts and the judicial process.
It is not exhaustive and is intended to provide temporary guideposts while more permanent guidance and policy are developed.

kp.k: Core adjudication should not be delegated to AI
kp.d: Conrad reports that the interim guidance cautions against delegating decision-making and case adjudication to AI, with particular caution for novel legal questions. It recommends independent human verification of all AI output and retains accountability with judges, Judiciary users and those approving AI use. Courts are also encouraged to define the permitted tasks for locally approved tools.
qs: The interim guidance cautions against delegating core judicial functions to AI, including decision-making or case adjudication, and it recommends that users exercise extreme caution especially if using AI to aid in addressing novel legal questions.

It recommends that users review and independently verify all AI-generated content or output, and it reminds judges and Judiciary users and those who approve the use of AI that they are accountable for all work performed with the assistance of AI.
More broadly, the guidance encourages courts to consider defining the tasks for which locally approved AI tools may be used.

kp.k: AI disclosure requires context-sensitive ethical consideration
kp.d: The guidance recommends considering whether and to whom AI use should be disclosed, rather than prescribing universal disclosure. Transparency policies should be considered alongside local rules, professional obligations, confidentiality, other ethical considerations and protection of judicial integrity.
qs: The guidance recommends that AI users consider whether the use of AI should be disclosed, to whom it should be disclosed, and whether transparency policies or practices are consistent with other ethical considerations, local rules, practices, professional obligations, confidentiality, and protecting the integrity of the Judiciary.

kp.k: Education and information sharing support responsible judicial adoption
kp.d: Conrad reports that, since the preceding year, the AO has circulated risk information concerning sensitive data, judicial opinions and procurement, as well as resources on litigants’ AI-assisted filings and materials from NIST’s Trustworthy & Responsible AI Resource Center. The Task Force is evaluating a possible Judiciary information-sharing site for local uses, rules and guidance; this remains a potential recommendation, not an established platform.
qs: In addition, background information, issues to consider, and resources regarding the use of AI tools for court filings by litigants has been provided.

Resources, including information provided by the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Trustworthy & Responsible AI Resource Center, have been provided to judges, court executives, and other Judiciary staff regarding the impact of artificial intelligence and related technologies on the work of the Judiciary.
The AI Task Force is evaluating and may recommend development of an online AI information sharing site for the Judiciary.

Such a site could potentially share information from courts, judges, chambers staff, and other Judiciary personnel on local uses of AI, as well as local rules, orders, policies, and guidance on AI use by judges, Judiciary personnel, and litigants.

kp.k: AI-generated evidence prompts two distinct evidentiary reform questions
kp.d: The Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on Rules of Evidence has considered AI-generated trial evidence since 2023. Conrad distinguishes ongoing consideration of authenticity rules for deepfakes from the question of regulating machine-learning opinion evidence when no expert witness is offered. The latter produced proposed Rule 707, published for public comment on August 15, 2025, with comments closing February 12, 2026, and hearings scheduled for January 15 and January 29, 2026; it is a proposal, not an enacted rule.
qs: The Advisory Committee has been considering this issue since 2023 and it was included in the agenda materials for the Advisory Committee’s May 2025 meeting, available via this link.

Specifically, the Advisory Committee is currently considering possible amendments to the Federal Rules of Evidence to address two evidentiary challenges: (1) whether changes to the authenticity rules are necessary to deal with “deepfakes”; and (2) whether a change is needed to give courts authority to regulate opinion evidence that is the product of machine learning when no expert witness is proffered to testify.
The Advisory Committee’s consideration of the first issue is ongoing.

The Advisory Committee’s consideration of the second issue resulted in a proposed new Rule 707, which was published for public comment beginning on August 15, 2025, with the comment period set to close on February 12, 2026.

kp.k: Other procedural AI reforms remain conditional
kp.d: As of the letter, no AI-related proposals were pending before the Civil, Criminal, Appellate or Bankruptcy Rules Advisory Committees. Conrad presents future attention as conditional on those committees determining that existing procedural rules inadequately address AI-related concerns in court proceedings.
qs: In addition, although there are no pending proposals to address AI concerns before the Advisory Committees on Civil Rules, Criminal Rules, Appellate Rules, and Bankruptcy Rules, this is an issue that may receive attention in the future if a determination is made by the appropriate Committees that existing procedural rules do not adequately address concerns raised by the use of AI in court proceedings.

kp.k: Existing disciplinary mechanisms address AI-related filing misconduct
kp.d: In discussing litigants’ AI use, Conrad identifies existing professional-conduct and procedural mechanisms rather than a new AI-specific sanctions regime. Canon 3B(6) calls for appropriate judicial action on reliable information suggesting attorney misconduct, potentially including state-bar referrals. Contempt powers and procedural rules also apply; Civil Rule 11 authorizes sanctions for deficient filings by attorneys or self-represented signatories.
qs: Regarding litigants’ use of AI, the Code of Conduct for U.S. Judges, at Canon 3B(6), provides that judges should “take appropriate action” if they have reliable information suggesting that an attorney has violated rules of professional conduct.
Such “appropriate action” may include making a referral to state bar disciplinary authorities.
In addition to the ability to refer concerns to state disciplinary authorities, judges have authority through their contempt power and the rules of procedure to address attorney misconduct.

For example, Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure authorizes judges to issue sanctions against attorneys or litigants (if self-represented and signing pleadings and motions on their own behalf) who file motions, pleadings, or other documents that fall below the standards set forth in Rule 11(b).

kp.k: National evidence on AI-related judicial enforcement remains anecdotal
kp.d: Conrad acknowledges anecdotal awareness of official judicial action concerning filing integrity where AI use was in question, but says such activity is not systematically tracked nationally. The AO collects attorney-sanctions data only in bankruptcy, annually publishing Rule 9011 statistics under 28 U.S.C. § 159(c)(3)(H). The letter therefore supplies neither a national count nor a measured rate of AI-related misconduct.
qs: The AO collects data relating to sanctions issued by judges against attorneys only in the bankruptcy context where the AO annually publishes statistics on Rule 9011 sanctions, as required by 28 U.S.C. § 159(c)(3)(H).
We are aware anecdotally of incidents in which judges have taken official action (such as those described above) relating to the integrity of court filings in which the use
of AI tools was in question, although we currently do not systematically track such activity at the national level.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Conrad describes increasingly common AI use in law and opportunities for the federal Judiciary, alongside risks to judicial integrity, confidentiality, and IT security.
pts.d: Conrad attributes growing use to general-purpose AI platforms and integration into legal research tools. He describes AI as transformative but does not specify measurable productivity benefits or predict employment or market effects.

pts.k: Conrad reports an augmentation-oriented approach: AI experimentation is permitted, but core judicial functions should not be delegated and humans remain responsible for checking outputs.
pts.d: These are recommendations in the Task Force’s interim guidance, as reported by Conrad, rather than empirical findings about AI performance or a categorical ban on judicial AI use. The approach preserves human decision-making, requires independent verification, and calls for particular caution on novel legal questions. Disclosure is presented as a contextual consideration rather than a universal requirement.

pts.k: AI-generated evidence raises authenticity and machine-learning opinion-evidence questions that are prompting consideration of federal evidentiary rule changes.
pts.d: Conrad reports ongoing consideration of deepfake authentication issues and a proposed Rule 707 addressing machine-learning opinion evidence when no expert witness is offered. The proposal is not described as an enacted rule. Changes to other procedural rules remain conditional on committees finding existing rules inadequate.

pts.k: A possible Judiciary-wide information-sharing site could support safer AI use in court administration and operations.
pts.d: Conrad presents this as a tentative institutional initiative, not an approved project or demonstrated benefit. The site could share local uses, rules, orders, policies, and guidance concerning AI use by judges, Judiciary personnel, and litigants.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies principally on institutional actions and legal authority; it offers no quantitative evidence of AI adoption, benefits, or error rates.
pts.d: Conrad supports the governance account with the Task Force’s guidance, AO information-sharing activities, and the Evidence Committee’s rulemaking process. For litigation misconduct, he cites Canon 3B(6), contempt powers, and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11. He reports anecdotal awareness of official action concerning filings where AI use was in question, but states that such activity is not systematically tracked nationally. The AO’s stated sanctions-data collection is confined to the bankruptcy context, not a national AI-specific dataset. No individual sanctions incident is described in the supplied text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The letter describes the position as of October 21, 2025, with temporary guidance and ongoing, conditional policy development.
pts.d: The interim guidance was circulated July 31, 2025, and is intended to bridge the period before more permanent guidance and policy. Evidence Committee consideration began in 2023. Proposed Rule 707’s comment period runs from August 15, 2025, to February 12, 2026, with hearings scheduled for January 2026. No deadline is given for permanent Judiciary AI policy or the possible information-sharing site. Other procedural rule changes are contingent rather than predicted with certainty.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are federal judges, chambers and court personnel, AI-use approvers, attorneys, and self-represented litigants.
pts.d: Judiciary personnel face oversight, verification, confidentiality, security, education, and procurement considerations. Judges retain responsibility for adjudication and AI-assisted work. Attorneys and self-represented filers remain subject to existing filing standards and potential sanctions. Parties presenting AI-generated evidence may be affected by future evidentiary rules. The source does not claim specific effects on law-firm staffing, fees, legal-service competition, or access to justice.
